text: The brown cuckoo-dove (Macropygia phasianella) is a dove in the genus Macropygia found in Australia, ranging from Weipa and Aurukun in the north to Bega in the south, and most inland at Atherton and Toowoomba. It is occasionally referred to as the "brown pigeon" or "pheasant pigeon," but these names are best avoided due to potential confusion with the brown doves and the true pheasant pigeon. It was one of three new species identified when the slender-billed cuckoo-dove was split in 2016. The species was formally described in 1821 by the Dutch zoologist Coenraad Jacob Temminck, based on a specimen collected near Port Jackson in New South Wales, Australia; he assigned it the binomial name Columba phasianella. The specific name derives from the Latin phasianus, meaning "pheasant," and is a diminutive form. The genus Macropygia was introduced by the English naturalist William Swainson in 1837. Three subspecies are recognised. The brown cuckoo-dove measures 40 to 43 centimetres (16 to 17 inches) in length, with feathers in a rich rusty-brown colour, and its short wings, long tail, and back are darker; males exhibit a slight rose/green colouration on their nape and neck. Its call is a loud "whoop-a whoop," with variations depending on the subspecies. It inhabits rainforest, woodland, scrubland, and rainforest regrowth areas. The doves are often seen in pairs or groups, feeding on berries from both native plants and introduced weed species; they can be nomadic, depending on food availability, and fly short distances low to the ground with great strength. Breeding occurs in spring and summer, with a nest constructed as a flat platform of sticks and vines, either in a tree fork or on top of a low tree, containing one creamy white egg.
